title: How can one area be written in two different ways?
description: A big rectangle of height v is split into two rectangles of widths four and three. The area is found from the whole width, and again by adding the two parts, and the two ways agree. Keeko's doubt is that four v plus three v is twelve v.
teaching_notes: One idea: the area of the big rectangle is seven v by its whole width, and four v plus three v by its parts, so the two must be equal. Watch for students who multiply the numbers in front of the letter instead of adding them.

source: A big rectangle of height v is split into two rectangles of
video_script.why: A learner sees why four v plus three v must equal seven v, from one area counted two ways.
video_script.substitution: the book's big rectangle of height v split into two rectangles of widths four and three, checked with v as two
video_script.anchor: the big rectangle of the book with height v, split into widths four and three
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies the numbers four and three instead of adding them. The widths add to make the whole width, so the idea is broken with v as two.
video_script.payoff_line: The area is seven v, and four v plus three v equals seven v

final_answer.spoken: seven v, and four v plus three v equals seven v

maths_rules: area of a rectangle = width x height
the two small areas are 4 x v = 4v and 3 x v = 3v
way 1: whole width = 4 + 3 = 7, so area = 7 x v = 7v
check with v = 2: 4 x 2 + 3 x 2 = 8 + 6 = 14 and 7 x 2 = 14
Keeko test with v = 2: 12 x 2 = 24, which is not 14
video_script.design: The split rectangle stays on the board; the area is found from the whole width and from the two parts, and the two results are set equal.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about the area of a big rectangle.
<bookmark mark='split'/>The height is v, and the rectangle is split into two parts of widths four and three.
<bookmark mark='areas'/>The areas of the two parts are four v and three v.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The book wants the area of the whole rectangle in two ways. What will it be?

beats.on_screen: the split rectangle stays on the board
narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a rectangle of width 4 and height v with area 4 × v = 4v

marks.rect: a rectangle of width four and height v appears
marks.rule: the words width times height are written
marks.write: 4 × v is written and shortened to 4v

narration: <bookmark mark='rect'/>The area of a rectangle is its width times its height.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>A part of width four and height v has area four times v.
<bookmark mark='write'/>Four times v is written as four v.

beats.on_screen: Given: height v; widths 4 and 3; areas 4v and 3v
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a rectangle of height v split into widths four and three.

beats.on_screen: To find: the area of the big rectangle in two ways

marks.find: the words area of the big rectangle are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the area of the big rectangle in two ways.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, way 1, use the whole width: 4 + 3 = 7, so area = 7 × v = 7v

marks.width: the widths 4 and 3 are joined along the bottom to give 7

narration: <bookmark mark='width'/>Step one, use the whole width, which is four plus three, or seven.
<bookmark mark='area'/>The area is seven times v, which is seven v.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, way 2, add the two parts: 4v + 3v

marks.parts: the two small areas 4v and 3v are lit in turn

narration: <bookmark mark='parts'/>Step two, add the areas of the two parts.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>The area is four v plus three v.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, both ways give one area: 4v + 3v = 7v; 4v and 3v are like terms; check v = 2: 8 + 6 = 14 and 7 × 2 = 14

marks.same: the two results are joined by an equals sign
marks.name: 4v and 3v are circled and the words like terms are written
marks.check: 2 replaces v and both sides show 14

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Step three, both ways measure the same area, so four v plus three v is seven v.
<bookmark mark='name'/>Four v and three v have the same letter-number v. We call such terms like terms.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Check with v as two. Eight plus six is fourteen, and seven times two is fourteen.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The area is seven v, and four v plus three v equals seven v.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the rectangle
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 12v, struck out; the test v = 2 gives 14 and 24

marks.gap: 14 and 24 appear side by side and do not match
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and 7v stays

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks four v plus three v is twelve v, because four times three is twelve.
<bookmark mark='test'/>Try v as two.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The two parts have areas eight and six, which make fourteen, but that idea gives twenty four.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The widths four and three are added to make the whole width, not multiplied.
